linux-command-line-sr1-02.reason: weak_card that had to be rewritten: dropping sr1-02, sr1-09 and sr1-11 would leave r1 at 3 true and 6 false. This uses the verifier's replacement, shortened to one fact. Confirmed in FHS 3.0 section 3.7: "No binaries may be located under /etc" and "it must be static and cannot be an executable binary". linux-command-line-sr1-02.statement: FHS forbids placing executable binaries under the `/etc` configuration hierarchy.
linux-command-line-sr1-02.explanation: FHS 3.0 limits /etc to static, local files that control how programs operate, and states that no binaries may be located under it.

linux-command-line-sr3-01.reason: source_problem: path_resolution(7) does not settle precedence when the owner is also in the group. acl(5) does. Its ACCESS CHECK ALGORITHM says that if the effective UID matches the owner, access is granted only if ACL_USER_OBJ contains the requested permissions, else denied. Its CORRESPONDENCE section says the owner permissions correspond to ACL_USER_OBJ. The statement now uses the verifier's clearer wording, which drops the clumsy 'can combine' and keeps False. (final: fixed)
linux-command-line-sr3-01.statement: Linux grants a file owner who is also in the file's group the union of the owner and group bits.
linux-command-line-sr3-01.explanation: Linux checks the owner class first: for the file's owner, only the owner permission bits decide access, even when the group bits would grant more.
linux-command-line-sr3-01.misconception: Owner and group permission bits combine when the owner belongs to the file's group.

linux-command-line-sr3-02.reason: source_problem: path_resolution(7) does not support the read-means-list half. The GNU coreutils Mode-Structure node supports both halves: "For directories, this means permission to list the contents of the directory" for read, and "permission to access files in the directory" for execute. gnu.org refused connections, so I read it through the Web Archive. The statement is unchanged and the explanation is aligned to the page. (final: keep)
linux-command-line-sr3-02.statement: A directory's read bit grants permission to traverse that directory during pathname lookup.
linux-command-line-sr3-02.explanation: For a directory, the execute bit grants access to the files inside it during lookup, while the read bit lets a user list the names it contains.
linux-command-line-sr3-02.misconception: Directory read permission also provides search permission.

linux-command-line-sr3-11.reason: source_problem: bash(1) never mentions the execute bit. The Bash manual's Shell Scripts node says Bash "reads and executes commands from the file" given as the first argument, and that a script "may be made executable" with chmod for running it through PATH (read through the Web Archive). The statement is reworded with the same fact and answer, which removes the true-card hedge 'can' and the 'even when' tell. (final: keep)
linux-command-line-sr3-11.statement: `bash script.sh` runs the commands in a readable script whose mode is 0644.
linux-command-line-sr3-11.explanation: Given as an argument, the file is opened and read by Bash, so read permission is enough. The execute bit matters when the script itself is run as a command, for example found through PATH.

linux-command-line-sr5-12.reason: source_problem: pidfd_open(2) only implies PID reuse. pidfd_send_signal(2) states it: "the originally intended target process has terminated and its PID has been recycled for another process". The explanation now matches that page; the statement is unchanged. (final: fixed)
linux-command-line-sr5-12.statement: Linux keeps a terminated process's PID reserved until the next system boot.
linux-command-line-sr5-12.explanation: Once a terminated process has been removed from the kernel process table, Linux can recycle its PID for another process, so a stored PID may later name an unrelated one.
linux-command-line-sr5-12.misconception: Process IDs remain reserved for the entire boot, even after the processes disappear.

linux-command-line-sr8-03.reason: source_problem: bash(1) does not state the search order. environ(7) PATH does: it is used by sh(1) and other programs, and "The list of prefixes is searched from beginning to end ... until a file with execute permission is found." The statement is unchanged and the explanation is aligned. (final: keep)
linux-command-line-sr8-03.statement: When Bash searches PATH for an executable, it chooses the last matching directory's executable.
linux-command-line-sr8-03.explanation: PATH is searched from beginning to end, and the first directory holding a matching file with execute permission wins, so earlier entries take precedence.
linux-command-line-sr8-03.misconception: Later PATH entries take precedence over earlier matching entries during a search.

linux-command-line-sr12-11.reason: ambiguous: 'leaving the boot offset unspecified' is also true of `-b <previous boot ID>`. The rewrite names a bare -b. journalctl.xml v262 says "The argument may be empty, in which case logs for the current boot will be shown" and "-1 the boot before last". I wrote 'bare' instead of the verifier's 'with no boot ID or offset' to avoid a negation. (final: keep)
linux-command-line-sr12-11.statement: Running a bare `journalctl -b` shows the log messages recorded during the previous boot.
linux-command-line-sr12-11.explanation: With an empty argument, journalctl -b shows the current boot. An offset such as journalctl -b -1 selects the boot before it.
linux-command-line-sr12-11.misconception: Omitting journalctl's boot argument selects the previous boot.
